summary: Jharkhand stands under India's national framework on gender recognition, criminal law, identity documents, entry and healthcare. No Jharkhand-specific deviation from the national position is sourced, so the national assessment governs what a trans visitor to the state should expect when dealing with police, passport and district authorities, and healthcare providers.
tangentialFactors:
India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, which removes self-identification from the 2019 law, restricts legal recognition to traditionally recognised groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex persons, and requires medical certification for identity recognition, reversing the 2014 Supreme Court ruling. The bill adds offences carrying up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring anyone to be transgender, which Human Rights Watch warns could criminalise support networks. Assent was pending as of late March 2026.

Of 487,803 census-recorded transgender persons in India, only about 32,500 hold identity cards.
localsOnly: Jharkhand residents seeking legal gender recognition must meet the national conditions set by the March 2026 amendment: membership of a traditionally recognised group such as hijra or kinner, or intersex status, together with medical certification. Self-identification alone no longer suffices under the amended national law.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Jharkhand-specific enforcement incidents, state welfare schemes, or state-level facilities for transgender persons were identified in the source inventory; the assessment rests on the national framework alone.

The commencement date and implementation of the March 2026 amendment, including whether presidential assent has been given, remain unresolved in the sources, which record assent as pending in late March 2026.
